title: The powerhouse that pulled Geary Street

place.label: Geary Street cable powerhouse site, NW corner of Geary & Buchanan

hook: A carpenter died building it. For 32 years it hauled cable under Geary. Then the city took the line over and started Muni.
story: In August 1879 a carpenter named Michael Rochfort was killed by a falling derrick while building an engine house at Geary and Buchanan for the new Geary Street cable road [1]. The line opened on 16 February 1880. From a two-storey wooden powerhouse on the northwest corner, a cable ran under Geary out toward Central (now Presidio) Avenue, and steam dummies sometimes carried riders further west [1][2]. By the 1900s Progressive reformers wanted the city to own its utilities, and riders were fed up with the slow little cars, which the Western Neighborhoods Project puts at six miles an hour [3]. Voters approved a city-run line on Geary in 1909 [1]. When the private franchise was not renewed, the last cable car left the Market Street turntable at 12:32 a.m. on 6 May 1912. Gripman F. Brainerd and conductor F. Stanley were aboard, and workmen were already ripping out cable behind them [1]. On 28 December 1912 Mayor James Rolph opened the city's electric A and B Geary lines, the first pieces of what became Muni [2][3].

title: Vaudeville under canvas at Post and Steiner

place.label: National Theatre site, NW corner of Post & Steiner

hook: Weeks after the city burned, the Graumans put a tent on a vacant lot and packed in thousands. Then they built the theatre around it without missing a show.
story: When the 1906 fire wiped out downtown's theatres, show business moved west to the parts of the city that had survived. On 28 May 1906 the National Tent Show Theatre opened on a vacant lot at the northwest corner of Post and Steiner, showing films and vaudeville. It was soon rebranded as Grauman's National [1]. Variety reported 2,400 people in the house that June [1]. In October 1906 the Examiner described a steel and iron building going up over the tent while three shows a day carried on, with 1,800 opera chairs planned [1]. The National was not alone. The Dreamland Rink behind it staged boxing by August 1906, and the Belascos' New Alcazar opened at Sutter and Steiner on 18 March 1907 [2][3]. Theatre historian Bill Counter warns that many Grauman legends conflict, including a hand-painted sign supposedly telling patrons that in another quake only the canvas would fall on them [1]. Some accounts, including Wikipedia's, put the first tent downtown on the site of the Graumans' old Unique Theatre. Counter says that was not the case [1][4].

title: Dreamland's floor that tilted

place.label: Dreamland Rink / New Dreamland Auditorium site, Steiner between Post & Sutter

hook: The old boxing barn closed on a knockout. Its $1 million replacement had a floor on hydraulic jacks that could lie flat for dances or tilt for opera.
story: For twenty years the Dreamland Rink, entered mid-block on the west side of Steiner, was the neighbourhood's big room. It held roller skating and boxing, and on the eve of the 1916 election Governor Hiram Johnson drew crowds so large that the theatre next door took the overflow [1]. By the 1920s, the city's Japantown report notes, Dreamland was also staging sumo wrestling [2]. The last event was a fight on 2 September 1927, when Ray Pelkey met Bert Colima. The Bulletin's Les Cohen quipped that the old rink and Pelkey "went out simultaneously" [1]. A new Dreamland Auditorium, designed by Ward & Blohme, went up across the rink and the old National Theatre lot. It opened in June 1928 [1][3]. The Examiner counted 8,500 seats for boxing and 4,500 for opera. The floor sat on hydraulic jacks so it could be level for dances or tilted for concerts [1]. The Examiner put the cost at $1.2 million. Wikipedia says $1 million, and opening dates vary between 26 and 29 June [1][3]. In 1939 the building was renamed Winterland [1].

title: Before the Fillmore, the Majestic

place.label: Majestic Hall (later the Fillmore Auditorium), Geary & Fillmore

hook: The hall where Hendrix and the Dead later played began as a mother-and-daughters venture, and it kept a colour line for more than forty years.
story: Decades before the psychedelic posters, the corner of Geary and Fillmore held a dance hall built by women. According to the city's Japantown historic context statement, Emma Gates Butler and her daughters built the Majestic Hall at the southwest corner in 1910. It was designed by the well-known architects James W. and Merritt Reid, who in 1911 also designed a five-storey building across Fillmore Street [1]. Other accounts give 1912 and describe the first tenant as the Majestic Hall and Academy of Dancing [2]. It was part of the entertainment boom that followed the 1906 quake, when Fillmore Street briefly became the city's downtown [1]. For a neighbourhood that was fast becoming one of the most mixed in the West, the Majestic kept a colour line. The same report notes that it was segregated until the 1950s [1]. The building went on to become the Ambassador Dance Hall in 1936 and a roller rink from 1939 to 1952. In 1954 the Black promoter Charles Sullivan took the lease, renamed it the Fillmore Auditorium and opened its doors to everyone [2].

title: When Fillmore Street was downtown
hook: With Market Street in ashes, City Hall, department stores and newspapers moved to Fillmore. Its boosters hung glowing iron arches over fourteen intersections.
story: The fire of April 1906 stopped at Van Ness Avenue, which left the Western Addition standing [1]. Almost overnight Fillmore Street became San Francisco's busiest shopping street [2]. The first streetcar to run after the disaster ran along Fillmore. City Hall, several department stores and newspapers set up on the street and the blocks around it [3]. The city's historic context statement says that in 1907 local boosters, hoping to keep Fillmore's new status, put up illuminated iron arches over fourteen intersections [3]. The arches can still be seen in photographs from around 1911 [1]. Nickelodeons followed. The Lyregraph, advertising "Moving and Talking Pictures", appears at 1730 Fillmore in the 1909 and 1911 city directories [4]. There was even a 1912 plan to tunnel under Fillmore to the Marina [1]. But once downtown was rebuilt, the offices and big stores went back. Fillmore settled into being a neighbourhood high street, and the old houses around it were divided up for the many families the fire had made homeless [1][3].

title: "A Greater San Francisco or Lesser Nagasaki?"

place.label: Post & Buchanan, heart of the new Nihonjin Machi

hook: In 1900 not one Japanese household lived here. Seven years later the Chronicle was warning of an "invasion." By 1910 this was the heart of Japanese San Francisco.
story: The 1900 census found no Japanese households in these blocks, which were then home to German, Irish and Jewish families [1]. The 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed the city's two Japanese enclaves, in Chinatown and along Jessie and Stevenson streets south of Market [1][2]. Refugees moved west, where some property owners of European descent were willing to rent to them. The newspaper Shin Sekai (New World) urged readers to settle for good, predicting that rents would fall once the ruined districts were rebuilt [1]. Not everyone welcomed them. On 24 March 1907 the San Francisco Chronicle ran an alarmist piece titled "A Greater San Francisco or Lesser Nagasaki – Which?" about the Japanese "invasion" of the Western Addition [1]. The community stayed anyway. By the 1910 census the core bounded by Bush, Geary, Webster and Laguna had more than 50 Japanese-owned businesses and most of the city's 4,700 Japanese residents [1]. There were pool halls, hotels and employment agencies for single men, and a kindergarten and midwives for new families. Yet the 1910 block book lists no Japanese property owners at all [1].

title: The school Issei parents built in protest
hook: San Francisco ordered 93 Japanese children into a segregated school. Their parents refused, opened their own classes on Post Street and started a diplomatic crisis.
story: On 11 October 1906 the Board of Education ordered the 93 Japanese students in its public schools to attend the segregated school it ran for Chinese children [1]. The Japanese community protested and alerted the press and officials in Japan, and Tokyo lodged a formal protest [1]. Here in the new Japantown, the city's historic context statement records, Issei parents set up the Sano School as a boycott measure, at 1761–65 Post Street [2]. The row became international. In his December 1906 message to Congress, Theodore Roosevelt called shutting Japanese children out of the public schools "a wicked absurdity" [1]. In January 1907 he invited the mayor and California officials to the White House. The city withdrew the order, and in return Roosevelt moved to cut Japanese immigration. That deal led to the 1907 Gentlemen's Agreement [1][2]. The Agreement still let wives and so-called picture brides come to join their husbands. Families grew, and with them this neighbourhood of Japanese schools, kindergartens and churches [2].

title: Barred from the Y, they built their own

place.label: Japanese YWCA / Issei Women's Building, 1830 Sutter Street

hook: Shut out of the city's YWCA, Issei women founded the nation's first independent Japanese YWCA, then raised money for a building the law barred them from owning.
story: In 1912 Japanese women were kept out of the facilities at San Francisco's main YWCA by segregationist policies. Issei women answered by founding the first independent Japanese YWCA in the United States [1]. Many of the women it served were newly arrived "picture brides" who had married men they knew only from photographs and letters. Its leading founder, Yonako (Yona) Abiko, aimed it at community, stability and job training [2]. The Y taught flower arranging and tea ceremony and organised concerts and socials [2]. After a short stay on Gough Street it moved to 1826 Sutter in the 1920s [3]. In 1928 Abiko launched a fundraising campaign for a building of its own on the site [2]. California's Alien Land Laws, passed in 1913 and 1920, meant Issei women could not own the building their own money paid for. So the San Francisco YWCA agreed to hold title in trust for the Nikkei community [1][2]. The Julia Morgan-designed building opened in 1932. The city's landmark report says it appears to be the only building in the United States purpose-built by and for Issei women [1].

title: Fish, pills and midwives on Post Street

place.label: Uoki K. Sakai Fish Market, 1684 Post Street

hook: A fish market with nine children upstairs across the road, the city's first Japanese pharmacy and a maternity hospital: one block of 1920s Post Street held a whole community.
story: By 1925 the Uoki K. Sakai Fish Market had moved from its first home on Geary, near Nikkei hotels, groceries and the Benkyo-do confectionery, to 1684 Post Street. The Sakai family took a big house across the street at 1628 Post, with room upstairs for their nine children [1]. By the late 1920s the north side of this block, between Buchanan and Laguna, also held the Nippon Drugstore, Namiye Murayama's Kinmon Maternity Hospital and the Gosha-do Books and Stationery store [1]. A few doors down at 1609 Post, a Mrs. Misawa ran what the city's history calls the first Japanese pharmacy registered in San Francisco [1]. Hatsuro Aizawa, whose father managed Gosha-do for owner Shoroku Ono, later remembered it as a place where people browsed and played cards even when they had no money to spend [1]. None of this was secure. The Alien Land Law kept most Issei from owning the buildings they traded in, so businesses often moved [1]. The Nippon Drug building later housed the jazz club Jimbo's Bop City and was eventually moved around the corner to Fillmore Street [2].

title: A widower's gift: Mount Zion on Post

place.label: Mount Zion Hospital, Hellman Building, 2200 Post Street

hook: When Esther Hellman died, her grieving husband gave $100,000 so San Francisco's Jewish hospital could rise again in the Western Addition. It is still treating patients.
story: Mount Zion was incorporated as a Jewish hospital in 1887 and opened ten years later at Sutter and Hyde, according to J. The Jewish News Weekly [1]. Historians William Issel and Robert Cherny place its first building on Sutter near Scott and date it to 1898 [2]. The Mount Zion Ladies' Auxiliary Society was central to the hospital, especially under Esther Hellman, wife of the banker Isaias Hellman [1]. When she died in 1908 he gave $100,000 for a new hospital in the Western Addition to be named after her. A UCSF librarian later remarked that it was remarkable the money was raised at all while the city was "in such a demolished state" [1]. Ground was broken in December 1911 and the cornerstone laid in 1912. The Hellman Building at 2200 Post opened in 1914 with room for 160 patients, and private wards cost $3 a day [1]. Issel and Cherny date the new building to 1913 [2]. It was part of a Jewish Western Addition that included synagogues, a Hebrew school and Sinai Memorial Chapel [2]. The building still stands and is now part of UCSF [1].

title: The newspaper that told Issei to stay

place.label: Nichibei Shimbun (Japanese American News), Laguna Street

hook: A former laundry owner made his Laguna Street paper the leading Japanese-language newspaper in America, and used it to urge immigrants to put down roots.
story: Kyutaro Abiko arrived in San Francisco in 1885, worked menial jobs and put himself through school and into UC Berkeley. He briefly ran a restaurant and a laundry [1]. In 1897 he took over a small paper, and in 1899 a merger created the Nichibei Shimbun (Japanese American News) [1]. After the 1906 fire it was one of two Japanese newspapers anchoring the new Japantown. The Nichibei was on Laguna Street and its rival, Shin Sekai (New World), was on Geary [2][3]. By 1910 the Nichibei led the field, and by the 1920s it had around 25,000 readers across the West [1]. Abiko used its pages to urge laborers to commit to permanent settlement and stable family life. In 1906 he founded a land company whose Yamato Colony near Livingston sold 40-acre plots to Japanese farmers [1]. Shin Sekai was less assimilationist and closer to the Buddhist community, and the two papers feuded for years [3]. After the 1924 Immigration Act, Abiko added an English section aimed at the Nisei and sponsored their study tours of Japan [1].

title: A square saved in 1855

place.label: Hamilton Square, west of Steiner between Geary & Post

hook: Before the Western Addition had houses it had a plan, and that plan set aside eleven public squares. One of them is still green here.
story: In the early 1850s San Francisco ended at Larkin Street. The young city claimed the land beyond, as far as Divisadero and eventually the ocean, and the district between Larkin and Divisadero north of Market became the Western Addition [1][2]. The Van Ness Ordinance of 1855–56 extended the downtown street grid across the district and reserved land for public use, including eleven public squares [1]. Hamilton Square, just west of Steiner Street, is the one closest to Japantown [1]. Houses soon followed. The city's population grew by more than 160 percent in the 1860s, from 56,802 to 149,473, and by the turn of the century builders had covered the new blocks with Italianate, Stick and Queen Anne homes [1]. Nearby on Geary near Scott, Hamilton Junior High, built in 1875 and demolished in 1930, had a student body that Jerry Flamm described as a mix of white, Black and Japanese children [3].
